items.t: ECB publishes consolidated banking data for end-June 2026
body: The European Central Bank (ECB) has published consolidated banking data as at end-June 2026, a dataset for the EU banking system compiled on a group consolidated basis.

The quarterly data provide information required to analyse the EU banking sector and comprise a subset of the information that is available in the year-end dataset. The data cover 336 banking groups and 2283 stand-alone credit institutions and non-EU controlled subsidiaries and branches operating in the EU, accounting for nearly 100% of the EU banking sector’s balance sheet. They include an extensive range of indicators on profitability and efficiency, balance sheet composition, liquidity and funding, asset quality, asset encumbrance, capital adequacy and solvency. Aggregates and indicators are published for the reporting population.

Reporters generally apply International Financial Reporting Standards and the European Banking Authority’s Implementing Technical Standards on Supervisory Reporting. However, some small and medium-sized reporters may apply national accounting standards. Accordingly, aggregates and indicators may include some data that are based on national accounting standards, depending on the availability of the underlying items.
In addition to data as of end-June 2026, the published figures also include a few revisions to past data.

items.t: Isabel Schnabel: Navigating stormy waters: reflections on monetary policy
body: The past seven years have been an extraordinary journey.[1]

We have moved from a world in which inflation was persistently too low to one marked by recurrent inflationary shocks; from a historically accommodative monetary policy stance to the fastest tightening cycle in the history of the ECB; and from a deeply integrated global economy to one increasingly shaped by fragmentation and geopolitical tensions.

As I reach the end of my journey here at the ECB, I would like to reflect on the lessons these experiences have taught me about the conduct of monetary policy in a world that has become less predictable.
My remarks today are personal reflections on how the experience of recent years has shaped my thinking about monetary policy and what it may teach us about navigating the challenges ahead.
The first takeaway is that central banks should prioritise instruments that allow them to adjust monetary policy quickly as conditions change.

We entered the pandemic after a long period in which inflation had been below our target (Slide 2, left-hand side). Globalisation, and the integration of China in particular, had structurally lowered the global cost of producing goods, putting downward pressure on inflation.

At the same time, the global financial crisis and the sovereign debt crisis had weakened public and private balance sheets and left lasting scars on demand, weighing on economic activity and inflation.
Over time, this experience gradually fostered the belief that these forces were permanent, leaving monetary policy primarily focused on bringing inflation back up to target.

As a result, after chronically overpredicting inflation before the pandemic, we were slow to recognise that we had entered a new regime in which we would repeatedly underpredict it (Slide 2, right-hand side).

Indeed, even as evidence of a more substantial and persistent rise in inflation was mounting, the initial reaction was one of relief: the economy finally seemed to be escaping the low-inflation environment.[2]
But the rapid increase in the share of goods and services experiencing inflation above 2% signalled that price pressures were becoming increasingly broad-based (Slide 3).
This exposed two key features of the inflation process that our analytical frameworks had not sufficiently accounted for.
One was the steepening of the Phillips curve, which was in part a result of more frequent price changes as firms sought to protect their profit margins in the face of sharp cost increases (Slide 4).

The other, related feature was the role of firms’ profits in inflation. Unlike the high-inflation period of the 1970s, when inflation was almost entirely driven by growth in unit labour costs, the post-pandemic inflation surge was to a significant extent driven by rising unit profits (Slide 5).[3]
So, the pandemic was a structural break in many of the trends we had witnessed before.
This included a shift in the global balance between savings and investment.

Rising investment needs related to the green and digital transitions, alongside a changing geopolitical environment, have turned the savings glut of the past into a bond glut, as both private and public issuance have increased sharply.[4]
This shift puts upward pressure not only on inflation but also on the natural rate of interest, r* (Slide 6, left-hand side).[5]

None of these shocks or their consequences could have been predicted easily. The lesson is therefore that we should expect the unexpected – and avoid becoming too attached to a particular view of the world or a particular class of models.
This has implications for the design and conduct of monetary policy.[6]
We should be wary of commitments that depend too heavily on a particular economic environment or class of models, leaving little room to adjust when conditions change.

Charles Goodhart – a distinguished scholar of monetary history who has seen the world change more than once – put it this way: “The world changes, and if the world changes you need sufficient flexibility to change the way that you operate within that.”[7]
In retrospect, forward guidance during the pandemic was too Odyssean. It tied our hands too closely to a world of persistently low inflation.

items.t: Piero Cipollone: Shaping the future of money
body: Money connects people and societies.
But to do this, it must be trusted. It must allow people and businesses to transact safely and efficiently. And it must evolve with geopolitical and technological developments.
For centuries, central banks have issued money and safeguarded its value. That mandate remains unchanged. But the environment in which money is used is being transformed.

People are increasingly paying digitally. Tokenisation could reorganise the financial value chain. New solutions are being considered to enhance cross-border payments. And geopolitical fragmentation is making the resilience and governance of critical infrastructure ever more important.
Central banks must therefore ensure that the money they issue remains fit for the future.

This does not mean replacing the private sector or predicting which technology will prevail. It means providing a trusted public foundation for payments and finance on which private innovation can flourish. And it means preventing digitalisation from increasing fragmentation or creating new dependencies.
This is why the Eurosystem has adopted a comprehensive payments strategy.[1]

The strategy has four objectives: ensuring that central bank money can continue to settle retail and wholesale transactions as preferences and technologies evolve; strengthening Europe’s resilience and strategic autonomy; fostering an integrated, competitive and innovative payments ecosystem; and supporting the international role of the euro.
In other words, we are seeking to comprehensively upgrade money and payments in Europe.

The Western Balkans are also taking active policy steps to enhance and integrate payments in the region. Several countries, including Albania, have already joined the Single Euro Payments Area. And a clone of the Eurosystem’s fast payment system (TIPS), developed by Banca d’Italia, is already fully operational in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Montenegro and will soon be launched in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia. It allows real-time, low-cost domestic transactions in local currencies around the clock, every day of the year.
This represents real, tangible progress that people will benefit from in their daily lives.
But we must always think one step ahead.
So today, I will discuss four key initiatives we are working on.
We are modernising euro banknotes.
We are developing a digital euro.
We are making it possible to settle tokenised asset transactions in central bank money and creating the conditions for an integrated and innovative tokenised finance ecosystem.
And we are interlinking fast payment systems to make cross-border payments faster and more efficient.
These initiatives have a common goal: ensuring access to safe public money while creating space for private innovation and international cooperation.
Let me begin with the most familiar form of central bank money: cash.

In discussions about digitalisation, cash is sometimes talked about as a technology of the past. That is a mistake. In an age where cyber risks, hybrid threats and system outages make the headlines, cash remains the most resilient form of payment we have.

More than 31 billion euro banknotes, worth over €1.6 trillion, are in circulation. People do not just see cash as a means of payment; they also view it as a store of value and a safeguard in periods of uncertainty. And it is one of the most tangible symbols of European unity.
Moreover, cash is inclusive and simple to use, as it does not require a device or an intermediary. It protects privacy. And, most importantly, it gives people freedom of choice.
That is why Europe is not choosing between cash and digital payments. We are investing in both.

The Single Currency Package reflects this approach.[2] Alongside the proposed Regulation on the establishment of a digital euro, it includes a proposed Regulation on the legal tender status of euro banknotes and coins. The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have adopted their respective positions, and the interinstitutional negotiations are under way.
But protecting cash is not enough. We must also prepare it for the future.

body: Data for goods on a Census basis are compiled from the documents collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and reflect the movement of goods between foreign countries and the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and U.S. Foreign Trade Zones. They include government and non-government shipments of goods and exclude shipments between the United States and its territories and possessions; transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic, and consular installations abroad; U.S. goods returned to the United States by its Armed Forces; personal and household effects of travelers; and in-transit shipments. The General Imports value reflects the total arrival of merchandise from foreign countries that immediately enters consumption channels, warehouses, or Foreign Trade Zones.

For imports, the value reported is the CBP-appraised value of merchandise—generally, the price paid for merchandise for export to the United States. Import duties, freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in bringing merchandise to the United States are excluded. The exception is exhibit 17a, which shows CIF import value. The CIF (cost, insurance, and freight) value represents the landed value of the merchandise at the first port of arrival in the United States. It is computed by adding import charges to the customs value and therefore excludes U.S. import duties.

Exports are valued at the f.a.s. (free alongside ship) value of merchandise at the U.S. port of export, based on the transaction price including inland freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in placing the merchandise alongside the carrier at the U.S. port of exportation.
Revision procedure (Census basis)

Monthly revisions: Monthly data include actual month's transactions as well as a small number of transactions for previous months. Each month, the U.S. Census Bureau revises the aggregate seasonally adjusted (nominal and real, or chained-dollar) and unadjusted export, import, and trade balance figures, as well as the end-use totals for the prior month. Country detail data and commodity detail data, based on the Standard International Trade Classification (SITC) Revision 4 and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), are not revised monthly. The timing adjustment shown in exhibit 14 is the difference between monthly data as originally reported and as recompiled.

For August 2026, unadjusted exports of goods were revised up $0.1 billion and unadjusted imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion. Goods carry-over in September 2026 was $0.8 billion (0.4 percent) for exports and $0.4 billion (0.1 percent) for imports. For August 2026, revised export carry-over was less than $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent) and revised import carry-over was $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent).

Quarterly revisions to chain-weighted dollar series: For March, June, September, and December statistical month releases, revisions are made to the real, or chained-dollar, series presented in exhibits 10 and 11: the previous five months are revised to incorporate the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' (BLS) revisions to price indexes, which are used to produce the real series and to align Census data with data published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the national income and product accounts (NIPAs).

Annual revisions: Each June, not seasonally adjusted goods data are revised to redistribute monthly data that arrived too late for inclusion in the month of transaction. In addition, revisions are made to reflect corrections received subsequent to the monthly revisions. Seasonally adjusted data are also revised to reflect recalculated seasonal and trading-day adjustments. These revisions are reflected in totals, end-use, commodity, and country summary data.

Other revisions: For December and January statistical month releases, each prior month of the most recent full year is revised so that the totals of the seasonally adjusted months equal the annual totals.

items.t: ECB wage tracker suggests slightly higher wage growth in first three quarters of 2027 compared with the full year of 2026
body: The European Central Bank (ECB) headline wage tracker, which covers active collective bargaining agreements with one-off payments smoothed over 12 months, indicates negotiated wage growth of 2.3% in 2026 (based on a coverage of 46.2% of employees in participating countries). The tracker stands at 2.7% for the second half of 2026 (based on a coverage of 45.6%) and 2.8% for the first half of 2027 (based on a coverage of 31.8%), and declines to 2.4% for the third quarter of 2027 (based on a still relatively low coverage of 23.3%). The relatively low ECB wage tracker in the first half of 2026 still reflects the downward mechanical impact of one-off payments that were initially paid in the second half of 2024 and not repeated in the following year. These effects dissipate fully in the second half of 2026.

Compared with the September 2026 data release, the headline wage tracker was revised upwards slightly for the second half of 2026 and for the first half of 2027, by around 0.1 percentage points on average.

The ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments stands at 2.4% for the third quarter of 2027, down from 2.7% for the first half of 2027 and for 2026 as a whole. The wage tracker excluding one-off payments moderates to 2.5% for the third quarter of 2027 from 2.9% for the first half of 2027 and stands at 2.6% on average for 2026, continuing to indicate a limited scope for one-off payments in recently signed collective bargaining agreements. Excluding one-offs, the ECB wage tracker averages 2.8% in the first three quarters of 2027, indicating a slightly higher permanent negotiated wage growth than registered for the full year of 2026.

The headline ECB wage tracker is better suited to describing quarterly or monthly dynamics in negotiated wages as it smooths one-off payments over time. By contrast, the ECB wage tracker with unsmoothed one-off payments is better suited to describing yearly dynamics in negotiated wages.

The forward-looking horizon of the wage tracker has been extended up to the end of September 2027. As new agreements are signed and coverage of contracts reaching 2027 gradually increases, the forward-looking horizon of the wage tracker will be further extended to the full year of 2027 in the December 2026 data release.

Employee coverage for 2026 stands at 46.2% but decreases significantly to 31.8% in the first half of 2027 and to 23.3% in the third quarter of 2027. The employee coverage is still limited for the third quarter of 2027 and will steadily increase over time as more wage agreements are signed. The employee coverage for 2026 and the first half of 2027 is broadly similar to that recorded at the same time last year, as indicated in the November 2025 data release. See Chart 1 and Table 1 for further details.

Overall, the ECB wage tracker may be subject to revision, and the forward-looking component should not be interpreted as a forecast, as it only captures information that is currently available for active collective bargaining agreements. Moreover, the ECB wage tracker does not perfectly track the indicator of negotiated wage growth, which is aggregated for the euro area based on country-level data on negotiated wage growth calculated by national sources (see Chart 1, left panel). Therefore, deviations from the indicator of negotiated wage growth are to be expected over time.

For a more comprehensive assessment of wage developments in the euro area, please refer to the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area, which indicate a yearly growth rate of compensation per employee of 3.3% in 2026.

The ECB publishes four wage tracker indicators for the aggregate of the nine participating euro area countries on the ECB Data Portal. The data release following the December 2026 meeting of the ECB Governing Council will exceptionally be published on 18 December 2026.

items.t: Boris Vujčić: Integrated, open and resilient: Europe’s strengths in a fragmenting world
body: Thank you to the Central Bank of Ireland for organising this conference and inviting me to speak. It is a great pleasure to be here in Dublin. Ireland illustrates why the topics of today’s event – from geopolitics to financial resilience – are timely.

Ireland has one of the most open economies in the world and it is deeply integrated into European and global markets. It is a Single Market success story, and a reminder that openness remains one of Europe’s greatest strengths.
But openness works both ways. A shift in US trade policy or a turn in global capital flows can spill over to the Irish economy particularly quickly.

What is true for Ireland is also true on a larger scale for the EU, the world’s largest trading bloc.[1] So, the question I would like to discuss today is simple to ask but harder to answer: how do we retain the benefits of an open economy in a more uncertain world increasingly shaped by geopolitics?
My answer in a single sentence is: not by retreating from openness, but by building the resilience that allows this openness to endure.
Let me start with the environment we are facing. Geopolitical shocks are becoming more frequent. They affect growth and inflation directly, and they can threaten financial stability.

We have seen this repeatedly in recent years. Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East have triggered severe disruptions in energy markets. Tariffs have renewed uncertainty and redirected global trade flows, while restrictions on exports of critical technologies and raw materials have reinforced the value of strategic autonomy (Slide 2, left-hand side). Alongside these developments, we have seen sanctions regimes, cyber threats and a step change in security and defence spending.

The result is a different macroeconomic environment. Inflation, for example, is now driven more often by supply shocks – in the past six years supply factors have played a role in three major shocks: in 2020, 2022 and 2026. And we are faced with more volatile energy prices as well as greater uncertainty about the outlook (Slide 2, right-hand side).

These shocks can also be transmitted through financial channels. Bond and equity prices may come under pressure, while investment funds could face outflows that amplify market movements.[2] Banks exposed to affected countries, sectors or markets may experience losses that weigh on capital or raise funding costs, potentially leading them to tighten lending.[3]

So far, the financial system has absorbed each of these shocks remarkably well. But financial effects can be highly non-linear and typically emerge abruptly: past resilience is no reason for complacency.

We cannot prevent geopolitical shocks. And pulling back from the world would not shield us from such shocks: while a fragmenting world means fewer links, it also means that those links are more concentrated. The result is less diversification and higher risk.
Energy is the clearest, and unfortunately a recurring, example.

The EU imports 57% of its energy, and almost all of its oil and gas. Before 2022, much of that came from Russia. That is why Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused the EU’s largest energy shock since the 1970s.

Europe responded. We diversified our energy supplies by increasing liquefied natural gas (LNG) import capacity and reduced our dependence on Russia. This is an important achievement. But diversification alone could not shield us when tensions erupted in the Middle East earlier this year.
This showed us that exposure is only half the story. The other half is about resilience – in other words, how well we absorb the shocks.
For the financial sector, resilience means strong capital and liquidity buffers, diversified funding, and payment and settlement systems that can withstand operational and cyber threats.

But there is also a broader, economy-wide dimension to resilience – one that is becoming increasingly important for Europe. In a more competitive and uncertain global environment, resilience requires stronger mechanisms for sharing risks and diversifying supply chains across countries and markets.

items.t: Philip R. Lane: AI adoption in Europe
body: San Francisco, 30 October 2026

My aim today is to describe how AI is reshaping the euro area economy.[1] Although the development of frontier AI models is primarily taking place in the United States and China, the adoption of AI will be a key determinant of European productivity growth in the coming years, while expenditure on AI adoption also currently constitutes a significant stimulus to the euro area economy.[2] In addition, European firms are part of the global AI supply chain, while European investors are contributing to the funding of the global buildout of AI infrastructure through equity and debt markets and the banking system.

I will also describe the key patterns we see in the data, with a primary focus on how the surveys conducted by the ECB can provide insights into the AI adoption process and the implications for the financial system.[3][4]

Digital investment in the euro area has expanded by 73 per cent in real terms since 2014, increasing from 2.3 per cent to 3.3 per cent of GDP (Chart 1a). While digital investment has grown far more quickly in the United States, the surge in digital investment (with an estimated clear acceleration since 2024) marks a distinct shift in the structure of the euro area economy.[5] As shown in Chart 1b, in the euro area digital investment has primarily been in intangible assets, while investment in data centres has constituted a relatively small share.[6]

In the ECB Corporate Telephone Survey, firms report that AI has added about 10 per cent to their capital expenditure plans this year. AI-related demand has helped activity to hold up over the last two years – as reflected by the contributions of the “computers and other electronics” and “information and communication services” sectors to total market production (Chart 2a). As illustrated in Chart 2b, Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) indicators show that output, employment and new orders have developed considerably more favourably in the technology equipment subsector than in other manufacturing subsectors. For services, the software subsector has performed better than other services sectors in terms of output, albeit not in terms of employment and new orders.

AI has been the main driver of global goods trade over the last year (Chart 3a). European firms are contributors to the global AI supply chain. Table 4 shows that AI-related exports and imports are growing quickly in the euro area, especially in relation to core data centre goods, which contain directly deployed hardware components related to AI compute, storage and networking capacity. Possibly related to differences in composition, the increase in AI import prices in the euro area is more muted than for the other major economic regions (Chart 3b). Chart 5 shows that, while AI-related price increases have contributed materially to the upward shift in goods inflation, the impact on headline inflation is limited owing to the relatively low weight of AI-exposed goods in the consumer price index (13.3 per cent in the non-energy industrial goods subcomponent and 3.4 per cent of the HICP).

In relation to trade in services, Chart 6 shows a significant upward movement in software licence imports from the United States since 2022, consistent with increased purchasing of AI licences from the leading US firms.[7]

European investors are also major purchasers of US technology-related equities (Chart 7). Listed European tech firms have also benefited from rising stock market valuations (Chart 8a). Stock returns, revenue growth, operating margin growth and earnings per share growth are all increasing in AI-intensity (Chart 8b).

US firms (especially the hyperscalers building out the AI infrastructure) have been large-scale issuers of euro-denominated bonds (reverse Yankees). So far, the available data show that purchases by European investors of euro-denominated bonds issued by US firms have increased alongside a decline in their purchases of US Treasury bonds (Chart 9a).[8]

Both agreements were subsequently signed by the respective parties.

On 1 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/30 at the request of the Belgian Minister for Finances and Pensions, in charge of the National Lottery and the Federal Cultural Institutions.

On 8 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/31 at the request of the Central Bank of Cyprus, in agreement with the Cypriot Ministry of Finance.

On 8 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Opinion CON/2026/32 at the request of the Slovenian Ministry of Finance.

On 22 October 2026 the Governing Council adopted Guideline ECB/2026/28 amending Guideline (EU) 2024/2941 on the legal framework for accounting and financial reporting in the European System of Central Banks (ECB/2024/31). The amending Guideline, which will be published on EUR-Lex in due course, enhances transparency regarding the Eurosystem’s financial performance via a new reporting format for the consolidated annual balance sheet of the Eurosystem that requires changes to the categorisation of content under the items “Sundry”, “Reserves”, “Accumulated losses carried forward” and “Profit/(loss) for the year”.
Appointment of the Chair of the Legal Committee (LEGCO)

On 29 October 2026 the Governing Council appointed Petra Senkovic, ECB Director General Legal Services as of 1 November 2026, as Chair of LEGCO as of that date. Ms Senkovic will succeed Chiara Zilioli, who is retiring from the ECB. This appointment runs until 31 December 2028 to coincide with the terms of office of the chairs of the other Eurosystem/ESCB committees, who were reappointed in November 2025 for a three-year period from January 2026 to December 2028.
Extension of the European System of Central Banks (ESCB) cooperation programme for strengthening the central bank capacities in the Western Balkans to the central banks of Moldova and Ukraine

On 8 October 2026 the Governing Council supported the extension of the ongoing third phase of the cooperation programme between the ESCB and the Western Balkans to also include the central banks of Moldova and Ukraine, and endorsed the related legal and contractual documentation. This cooperation programme, coordinated by the Deutsche Bundesbank and financed by the European Commission under its Instrument for Pre-Accession Assistance (IPA III) Programming Framework for the period 2021-27, involves 21 ESCB national central banks and the third phase started in 2026 for a three-year period. As a result, the Western Balkans Phase III programme will consist of two regional components: the “Regional Component Moldova and Ukraine” and the “Regional Component WB6” for the ongoing programme for the Western Balkans.

items.t: Results of the ECB Survey of Professional Forecasters for the fourth quarter of 2026
body: Respondents’ expectations for headline inflation, as measured by the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP), stood at 3.0% for 2026, 2.6% for 2027 and 2.0% for 2028. Compared with the previous round, these were revised up by 0.3 and 0.4 percentage points for 2026 and 2027 respectively but remained unchanged for 2028. Longer-term expectations (for 2031) remained at 2.0% for both headline and core inflation. A special question, which was also asked in the previous round, concerned the impact of the war in the Middle East. The responses suggested that additional effects of the energy price shock are mainly expected for 2027 but that second-round effects will remain limited. For inflation, the risk balance was tilted to the upside for 2026-28 but remained more balanced thereafter.

Respondents expected real GDP growth of 1.0% in 2026 and 1.3% in both 2027 and 2028. Expectations were revised up by 0.4 percentage points for 2026 and by 0.1 percentage points for 2027 compared with the previous survey and were unchanged for 2028. Longer-term growth expectations (for 2031) were revised up by 0.1 percentage points to 1.3%. For real GDP growth, the balance of risks was tilted somewhat to the downside for all horizons.
Unemployment rate expectations were slightly higher for 2026 at 6.4%, before declining gradually to 6.1% in the longer term.

items.t: Piero Cipollone: Next-day securities settlement, tokenisation and the transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure
body: Frankfurt am Main, 29 October 2026
We are approaching an important milestone.[1]

Less than a year from now, on 11 October 2027, Europe will move to T+1 settlement. This means that the time from the moment a security is traded to the moment the buyer receives it and the seller is paid will be reduced from two days to one.
This may sound like a technical change, but it is in fact much more significant.

The transition to T+1 is part of a broader transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure. And the objective is clear: to make Europe’s financial and payment system more efficient, more resilient and safer, and ultimately to make European financial markets more competitive.
In the Eurosystem, we are contributing to this transformation across the full spectrum of our mandate.

We are ensuring that banknotes remain available and fit for purpose. We are preparing for a digital euro. We are modernising wholesale payments and securities settlement. And we are working to enhance cross-border payments and harness new technologies such as distributed ledger technology (DLT).[2]
These are not separate projects. They are different parts of the same strategy: ensuring that the euro and Europe’s financial markets are fit for the future in a rapidly changing world.
The move to T+1 contributes to this broader strategy.
It is about more than just reducing the time between trade and settlement to one day.
A shorter settlement cycle can reduce market and counterparty risk.

But, perhaps even more importantly for Europe, the transition is also forcing us to review our post-trade processes. It requires greater standardisation, automation and innovation. Inefficiencies that could be accommodated in a T+2 environment will become much more difficult to sustain under T+1.
In that sense, T+1 is a catalyst for modernising European post-trade markets. And this is important for Europe’s competitiveness.

Efficient post-trade infrastructure makes it easier for capital to flow across borders. It helps investors access European markets. And it supports the EU’s wider ambition to create deeper and more integrated capital markets.
It also ensures that Europe keeps pace internationally with other major markets as they shorten their own settlement cycles.
That is why the ECB, together with the European Securities and Markets Authority and the European Commission, strongly supports the market’s preparations for T+1.
There is another lesson for Europe here which I believe is particularly important: we can deliver when we work together.

Europe’s financial landscape remains complex and fragmented. Yet the work coordinated by the EU T+1 Industry Committee has shown that those differences do not need to stand in the way of common solutions.

I would therefore like to congratulate everyone involved for the progress made so far. It is a powerful reminder of what Europe can achieve when public authorities and the private sector come together around a common objective.
But we have not yet crossed the finish line.
The coming months will be critical. Implementation and testing need to advance with the same determination and cooperation that have been the driving force behind the project so far.

The Eurosystem is also responsible for operating TARGET2-Securities (T2S), our platform for securities settlement in central bank money through which cash and securities can be exchanged simultaneously across Europe.[3]
And the key message here is a simple one: T2S already supports shorter settlement cycles. It already settles substantial volumes of transactions on a T+1 and even a T+0 basis.
So we are not starting from scratch.

At the same time, we are adapting some T2S processes to help the market operate efficiently under the tighter timetable that T+1 will bring. This includes changes to the night-time settlement process, which are planned for June 2027 ahead of the market’s migration to T+1 settlement in October 2027.
We will continue working closely with market participants and other European authorities to ensure that the transition to T+1 settlement goes smoothly.
But while we prepare for T+1, we also need to look further ahead.

items.t: Christine Lagarde, Boris Vujčić: Monetary policy statement (with Q&A)
body: Frankfurt am Main, 29 October 2026
Good afternoon, the Vice-President and I welcome you to our press conference.

The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook. While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage. The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth. Financing conditions have tightened since our last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth. We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target in the medium term.

We remain well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty. We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular, our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.
The decisions taken today are set out in a press release available on our website.
I will now outline in more detail how we see the economy and inflation developing and will then explain our assessment of financial and monetary conditions.

The incoming data suggest that the euro area economy continued to expand in the third quarter of the year. Services have recovered, after weakening at the start of the Middle East conflict. Manufacturing, digital services and exports are benefiting from AI-related business investment. Government spending on infrastructure and defence is also supporting activity. These factors should continue to underpin growth in the near term. At the same time, renewed energy price increases have hit consumer confidence, and higher financing costs are likely to weigh on growth.
The unemployment rate remained at 6.4 per cent in August. Growth in employment and the labour force remains subdued, while productivity has gradually picked up.

Over the medium term, a recovery in confidence and real incomes, driven by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, should bolster domestic demand. Investment in AI-related activities and government spending on infrastructure and defence should also continue to support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand.

Higher potential growth requires structural reform and has to be underpinned by sound public finances. Fiscal sustainability is a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. Fiscal responses to the energy shock should be temporary, targeted and tailored. Simplifying and harmonising rules across the EU’s Single Market, accelerating the energy transition and completing the savings and investments union are key building blocks to make our economy more dynamic and resilient. As the process for agreeing on the legal framework for the digital euro moves into its final stage, we reiterate the importance of reaching agreement on the Single Currency Package as quickly as possible.

Inflation rose to 3.8 per cent in September, from 3.2 per cent in August. Energy price inflation increased markedly, to 18.9 per cent, from 14.3 per cent in August. Diesel and petrol prices reached new peaks in September, in part reflecting elevated refining margins. Inflation excluding energy increased to 2.3 per cent in September, from 2.1 per cent in August. Food price inflation increased to 1.3 per cent, from 1.1 per cent. Services inflation increased to 3.2 per cent in September, from 3.0 per cent in August, while goods inflation declined to 1.1 per cent from 1.2 per cent.

Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.

Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 4.9 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 4.6 percent in the second quarter.

The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 3.0 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 5.6 percent in the second quarter. body: Personal income increased $54.5 billion (0.2 percent at a monthly rate) in September, according to estimates released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). Disposable personal income (DPI)—personal income less personal current taxes—increased $52.7 billion (0.2 percent), and personal consumption expenditures (PCE) increased $113.1 billion (0.5 percent).

Personal outlays—the sum of PCE, personal interest payments, and personal current transfer payments—increased $113.0 billion in September. Personal saving was $911.1 billion, and the personal saving rate—personal saving as a percentage of DPI—was 3.8 percent.
The increase in current-dollar personal income in September primarily reflected increases in compensation and government social benefits.
The $113.1 billion increase in current-dollar PCE in September reflected increases of $35.1 billion in spending on goods and $78.1 billion in spending on services.
Real PCE increased $2.6 billion (less than 0.1 percent at a monthly rate) in September.
From the preceding month, the PCE price index for September increased 0.5 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 0.3 percent.
From the same month one year ago, the PCE price index for September increased 3.6 percent. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 3.1 percent from one year ago.

items.t: October 2026 euro area bank lending survey
body: According to the October 2026 bank lending survey (BLS), euro area banks reported a further net tightening of credit standards – banks’ internal guidelines or loan approval criteria – for loans or credit lines to enterprises in the third quarter of 2026 (net percentage of 9% of banks; Chart 1). Banks reported unchanged credit standards for loans to households for house purchase (net percentage of 0%) and a further net tightening for consumer credit and other lending to households (net percentage of 14%).

For firms, the net tightening surpassed the expectations reported by banks in the previous survey round (5%). Heightened risk perceptions and banks’ reduced risk tolerance remained the main drivers of tighter credit standards, with some banks reporting increasing pressure as a result of geopolitical uncertainty and energy developments. In a dedicated question on the importance of new lending to finance firms’ adoption or development of artificial intelligence (AI), banks indicated that they are still adapting their lending practices to the growing use of these technologies. Most reported that they had not yet introduced specific quantitative criteria for assessing AI-related lending within their credit standards. A small number noted that AI adoption and its associated risks increasingly feature in qualitative borrower assessments, with IT firms subject to the closest scrutiny. Banks reported broadly unchanged credit standards for housing loans and a further net tightening of credit standards for consumer credit. For housing loans, banks had expected a slight net tightening. Meanwhile, the tightening of credit standards for consumer credit exceeded banks’ expectations, owing mainly to lower risk tolerance and heightened risk perceptions. For the fourth quarter of 2026, banks expect credit standards to tighten further for firms and tighten significantly for both housing loans and consumer credit.
Banks’ overall terms and conditions – the actual terms and conditions agreed in loan contracts – tightened for all loan segments, driven mainly by higher interest rates.

Banks reported a net increase in the share of rejected loan applications for all borrower groups. The net increase in the share was higher for consumer credit than for loans to firms and housing loans.

In the third quarter of 2026, euro area banks reported a net decrease in demand for loans or credit lines to firms (net percentage of -6%; Chart 2). This net decline stood in contrast to banks’ expectations of an increase in the previous survey round (4%) and followed a small net increase in the second quarter (3%). Loan demand was primarily dampened by the general level of interest rates. Weaker demand for fixed investment among small and medium-sized enterprises and the move towards alternative sources of finance also weighed slightly on loan demand. Some banks reported that uncertainty regarding geopolitical and energy developments continued to suppress corporate loan demand, while upward pressure came from demand for inventories and working capital. When asked about the impact of AI adoption on demand, several banks indicated that they expect a gradual but sustained increase in loan demand to finance digital infrastructure, particularly data centres. Banks also reported that their current and prospective AI-related lending is more likely to target infrastructure providers than software developers or firms adopting AI, with this focus expected to become more pronounced over the coming months.

items.t: Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises: lending conditions tightened
body: In the most recent round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE) in the euro area, covering the third quarter of 2026, euro area firms widely reported a further net increase in interest rates on bank loans (net 46%, compared with 42% in the previous quarter). Large firms reported increases more often (net 55%, up from 41%) than small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) (net 38%, down from 43%). At the same time, a net 27% of firms (down from 31% in the previous quarter) reported increases in other financing costs (i.e. charges, fees and commissions) and in collateral requirements (net 14%, up from 10%) (Chart 1).

In this survey round, firms reported that the availability of bank loans had declined by more than their needs. Firms reported a decrease in the availability of bank loans in the third quarter of 2026 (-5%, compared with a net -1% in the second quarter of 2026), with both SMEs (net -5%, compared with -4%) and large firms (net -6%, down from 4%) reporting lower availability. At the same time, a net 2% of firms reported a decrease in their bank loan needs, while a net 2% reported an increase in the previous quarter. Developments in needs differed by firm size: SMEs reported broadly unchanged needs (net 1%, compared with 2%), while large firms reported a decrease (net -6%, down from 3%). As a result, the bank loan financing gap indicator, which captures the difference between changes in the need for and the availability of bank loans, was positive (net 2%, compared with 3% in the previous quarter) (Chart 2). Looking ahead, more firms expect the availability of external financing to decrease over the next three months.

Firms continued to perceive the general economic outlook as the main factor constraining the availability of external financing (net 31%, compared with 29% in the previous survey round), with large firms now more pessimistic than SMEs (net 35% and 29%, respectively). In this survey round, a net 9% of firms indicated that their firm-specific outlook, in terms of sales and profits, had a negative impact on the availability of external financing (after 10% in the previous survey round), while the impact of their capital position and creditworthiness remained positive.

The substantial change in the sample composition in this survey round, with first-time respondents accounting for the majority of the sample, makes it challenging to interpret the responses to the numerical questions at this stage. The increase in selling price expectations was contained among firms that took part in both this round and the previous one, whereas selling price expectations rose significantly in the full sample (Chart 3).

Similarly, firms’ median inflation expectations remained broadly unchanged among firms that took part in both the current and previous survey rounds, whereas they rose significantly in the full sample (Chart 4). The risk assessment for firms’ five-year-ahead inflation outlook was broadly unchanged.

The report published today presents the main results of the 40th round of the SAFE for the euro area. The survey was conducted between 26 August and 2 October 2026. In this survey round, around half of the firms were asked about changes in the period between July and September 2026. The remainder were asked about changes in the period between April and September 2026. Additionally, firms reported their expectations for euro area inflation, selling prices and other costs. The sample comprised 12,822 enterprises in the euro area, of which 11,917 (93%) had fewer than 250 employees.

items.t: Frank Elderson: Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
body: It is a pleasure to open the Finance and Biodiversity Day at COP17.
The theme of this COP is “Taking Action for Nature’’.
We have talked about the need for action for long enough. Now we need to act.
Four years ago, the international community adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, setting out a pathway to living in harmony with nature by 2050.
The destination is set. The path is clear. But progress has remained limited. And nature has not stood still. It has continued to deteriorate. So we need to accelerate.
Tangible progress requires a shift from targets to implementation, from awareness to engagement, from ambition to investment.
COP17 must help us accelerate the journey. And finance has a central role to play. That should not come as a surprise: without investment, there can be no transition.

But we need to get the economics right. Protecting and restoring nature is not simply spending. It is investment: investment in the natural capital on which our economies depend, investment in resilience, and investment in our future prosperity.
That is why Finance and Biodiversity Day matters.
Let me start with a fundamental question: why is nature so important to the economy?
We tend to think of roads, bridges and electricity grids as critical assets that serve as the foundation of a modern economy.
But there is another kind of infrastructure that we often take for granted: natural capital.

Nature provides services without which large parts of our economies could not function. Water keeps our factories and farms running, healthy soils sustain our food systems, forests and wetlands regulate droughts and floods, oceans absorb heat and carbon.
The World Bank estimates that as much as half of the world’s GDP relies on biodiversity, natural capital and ecosystem services.[1]

Our own analysis shows that 72% of companies in the euro area depend on at least one ecosystem service. And 75% of euro area corporate lending goes to companies that are highly dependent on at least one ecosystem service.[2]
The message is clear: nature is not peripheral to economic activity. It is fundamental to it.

But even as we speak, the foundations of our economies are being depleted at an alarming rate.[3] When ecosystems deteriorate, firms face higher costs, lower productivity and supply chain disruptions.
For far too long, we have treated nature as though it were free and inexhaustible. It is neither.
We have mistaken the depletion of natural capital for economic prosperity.
But we rarely – if ever – counted the soils depleted, the water systems stressed, the forests weakened or the ecosystems lost in producing it.
In economic terms, we have been consuming our capital and calling it income.

Nature is already presenting us with the bill. Depleted natural capital is already disrupting production, damaging supply chains and increasing costs. The consequences are already spreading from ecosystems to firms, from firms to balance sheets and from balance sheets into the financial system.
This is not a future tragedy on the horizon. It is an economic reality unfolding around us.
That is why taking action for nature is not only an environmental imperative.
It is an economic and financial necessity because our future prosperity directly depends on it.

Water is perhaps the clearest example of what happens when we fail to account for natural capital. For too long, we have allowed our economies to function as though reliable supplies of clean water were an unlimited production input. But an economy cannot negotiate with an empty river, a depleted aquifer or a failed ecosystem. When we withdraw water faster than it can be replenished, we are not creating prosperity. We are fooling ourselves and failing future generations by consuming the capital on which future prosperity depends.

Think about this summer’s heat-exacerbated drought conditions throughout Europe: major rivers, like the Rhine, Loire, Po and Danube, reached exceptionally low levels, forcing, among other things, the shutdown of critical nuclear power plants, while also negatively affecting hydropower and disrupting supply chains.[4]
